CHIEF COMPLAINT
Upper respiratory infection symptoms.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Andrew is a 59-year-old male with a past medical history of depression, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension who presents with symptoms of an upper respiratory infection.

Over the past week or so, while doing yard work and landscaping, he began to feel very tired and short of breath. He reports he has not been wearing masks as much at the end of the summer and thinks he caught his first cold, which then worsened. The shortness of breath occurs mainly with exertion, such as lifting or carrying heavy bags of soil, and he became very winded. He has not had shortness of breath at rest. He has not yet had a productive cough but feels it may be coming. He felt a little warm but attributed this to exertion. He reports bilateral elbow pain and tired knees with some tension around the knees, which he thinks is largely related to lifting the bags. He has received both COVID vaccines. He has no history of seasonal allergies. He has no known exposures.

Depression: He reports it has been a crazy year and a half, and he was somewhat concerned, but for the most part he is doing well. His wife got him into barre classes to help him relax, and he feels this is helping. He has previously discussed with his physician not starting medication for depression because he is on medications for other conditions.

Type 2 diabetes: He monitors his blood sugars on workdays during the week but usually forgets on weekends. His diet has been good for the most part, except for occasional house parties. His sugars have not been elevated since this illness began.

Hypertension: He monitors his blood pressure at home on workdays but not regularly on weekends. He reports it has been under control. He is taking his medication. He needs a refill of lisinopril.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for fatigue. Felt slightly warm, attributed to exertion. 
Respiratory: Positive for exertional shortness of breath. No cough productive of sputum yet.
Gastrointestinal: Negative for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for bilateral elbow pain and knee tiredness/tension.
Psychiatric: Depression, doing well overall.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Depression
Type 2 diabetes
Hypertension

MEDICATIONS
Metformin (dose prior to today not specified)
Lisinopril 20 mg daily

PHYSICAL EXAM
Vitals: Within normal limits. Afebrile.
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds strong.
Respiratory: Scattered rhonchi bilaterally that clear with cough.
Musculoskeletal: Pain to palpation of bilateral elbows.
Extremities: Mild edema of the lower extremities.

RESULTS
Chest x-ray: No airspace disease. No pneumonia.
Hemoglobin A1c: 8, elevated.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Upper respiratory infection, likely viral syndrome.
- Send COVID test to confirm negative, though suspicion is low given no known exposures.
- Expect resolution in a couple of days.
- Robitussin for cough.
- Ibuprofen or Tylenol as needed for fever.
- Patient to report if symptoms worsen.

2. Depression.
- Doing well with barre classes.
- Offered medication or referral to psychotherapy; patient declined at this time and would like to revisit in a few months.

3. Type 2 diabetes.
- Hemoglobin A1c is 8, above the goal of 6 to 7.
- Increase metformin to 1000 mg twice daily.
- Repeat hemoglobin A1c in 4 months (ordered).

4. Hypertension.
- Well managed.
- Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily; refill ordered.
- Order lipid panel.

Follow-up: Return in about 4 months. The nurse will assist with scheduling.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Annual exam.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Andrea is a 52-year-old female with a past medical history significant for rheumatoid arthritis, atrial fibrillation, and reflux who presents today for her annual exam. She was last seen one year ago.

Rheumatoid arthritis: She has been walking, exercising, and doing yoga, which she feels has helped her arthritis a lot. She has had no joint pain, stiffness, or flare-ups over the past year. She continues to take methotrexate once weekly without any issues.

Atrial fibrillation: She continues to have palpitations and has been in and out of atrial fibrillation over the past year or so. Her last episode was about a week ago. She has noticed that palpitations flare up when she becomes stressed. She has tried meditation and running with her dog to relieve stress, without much benefit. She called last month, and an event monitor was placed.

Reflux: She is taking Protonix and has made dietary modifications, including cutting out soda. She feels both have helped. She has not had a flare-up in about five months.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No complaints.
HEENT: Positive for nasal congestion due to allergies.
Cardiovascular: Positive for palpitations. Negative for chest pain.
Respiratory: Negative for shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: Negative for nausea or vomiting.
Musculoskeletal: Negative for joint pain or stiffness.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Rheumatoid arthritis
Atrial fibrillation
Reflux

MEDICATIONS
Methotrexate once weekly
Protonix 40 mg daily

PHYSICAL EXAM
Vitals: Heart rate well controlled.
Cardiovascular: Slight 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously noted. Regular rate and rhythm.
Respiratory: Lungs clear.
Musculoskeletal: Right elbow with edema and erythema, and pain to palpation. No lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Event monitor: Patient is in and out of atrial fibrillation with a conversion pause (pause after atrial fibrillation before return to regular rhythm).

Autoimmune panel: Within normal limits; consistent with well-controlled rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Rheumatoid arthritis
- Well controlled on methotrexate, with a reassuring autoimmune panel.
- Continue methotrexate 2.5 mg once weekly. Refill ordered.
- Patient may request a referral back to rheumatology if needed; currently stable.

2. Atrial fibrillation
- Paroxysmal, going in and out of atrial fibrillation with a conversion pause on event monitor. Palpitations are triggered by stress.
- Goal is to maintain normal sinus rhythm. Given her age and the paroxysmal pattern, will refer to cardiology for cardiac ablation. The procedure was explained as mapping where the rhythm originates and ablating that area to prevent recurrence.
- Referral to cardiology ordered.

3. Reflux
- Well controlled, with no flare-ups in about five months.
- Continue Protonix 40 mg daily.
- Continue dietary modifications, including avoiding coffee and spicy foods.
- Patient to report any further issues.

Emergency room follow-up for hyperglycemia.

He went to the ER over the weekend after feeling woozy and not keeping up with his blood sugar readings. His wife encouraged him to be evaluated. His blood sugar was found to be elevated. He was not admitted. His mother was hospitalized the previous week after a fall requiring hip replacement, and the patient and his wife had been eating cafeteria and fast food without monitoring his diet. He felt much better by the time he got home from the visit and reports he has since been following his diet closely. Before this episode, he was doing fine with his diet during the week because he is busy, but is less consistent on weekends when he is socializing and having people over.

Kidney transplant: He reports being diligent with his immunosuppressive medications. He last saw Dr. Reyes about 3 weeks ago, at which time everything seemed fine and kidney function was good.

Depression: He reports the past year and a half has been tough, but he is doing pretty well. He has some moments, but finding time to relax in the afternoon helps. Medical therapy has previously been deferred because of his many other medications. He prefers to avoid therapy at this time. His wife introduced him to meditation, which he finds relaxing, and he would like to continue it for a couple more months.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain.
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath.
Neurological: Denies lightheadedness and dizziness.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Depression
Type 2 diabetes
Kidney transplant

MEDICATIONS
Immunosuppressive medications (managed by Dr. Reyes)
Lantus (insulin glargine)

PHYSICAL EXAM
Vitals: Pulse oximetry, blood pressure, and heart rate within normal limits.
General: No acute distress.
Neck: No carotid bruits.
Cardiovascular: Slight 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously noted.
Respiratory: Lungs clear.
Extremities: 1+ lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Glucose: approximately 162 (patient had not eaten before the visit).
Hemoglobin A1c: approximately 8, mildly elevated.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
62-year-old male with type 2 diabetes, depression, and kidney transplant presenting for ER follow-up after a hyperglycemic episode.

1. Hyperglycemia / type 2 diabetes
- Episode likely related to dietary changes while caring for his mother. A1c of about 8 indicates blood sugars have been somewhat elevated overall.
- Increase Lantus to 20 units at night.
- Continue monitoring blood sugars and report readings; further adjustment may be needed.
- Repeat hemoglobin A1c in a couple of months (ordered).

2. Depression
- Doing well with current strategies, including meditation.
- Hold off on medication or therapy at this time.
- Patient to call if he needs anything.

3. Kidney transplant
- Kidney function stable.
- Patient to follow up with Dr. Reyes for management of all immunosuppression medications. Dr. Reyes will contact this provider if needed.
